title: Dog Microbes at Home Keep Babies Healthier — Study
paragraphs: Many parents worry that having a dog at home could bring germs that might harm their baby. However, a new study from Finland suggests that some of the microbes that dogs bring into the home may actually help keep babies healthy.

The study was carried out by researchers at the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare, Kuopio University Hospital and the University of Eastern Finland, and it was published in the journal Pediatric Allergy and Immunology in 2026. The first author was Jenni Mäki, a pediatrician and doctoral researcher. The researchers used data from a long-term study of nearly 400 families in Finland. About a third of the families lived on farms, half lived in the countryside and the rest lived in towns. The researchers measured the bacteria and fungi in dust collected from the families' homes and followed the children's health during their first year of life.

The researchers found that certain microbes linked to dogs were associated with fewer respiratory infections, fewer courses of antibiotics and more healthy weeks during the children's first year. These benefits remained even after the researchers took into account factors such as family size, where the families lived and exposure to tobacco smoke.

Interestingly, homes with dogs generally had a greater variety of microbes. However, this variety by itself was not linked to fewer infections. Instead, it was specific microbes, or combinations of them, that seemed to matter. These microbes explained up to a quarter of the protective effect of owning a dog.

According to Anne Karvonen, a chief researcher at the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare, respiratory infections in early childhood are a significant risk factor for asthma. Karvonen suggested that if dog-related microbes help prevent some of these infections, they might also reduce the risk of asthma later in life. However, this was not tested in the study.

The researchers pointed out that the study only shows a link and cannot prove that the microbes directly protect children. In addition, they did not examine other differences between families with and without dogs. For example, dog owners may spend more time outdoors.
